tier_reason: readme.md tables give cycles/32 elements for fmath vs std (logf 6.72 vs 105.20 = 15.7x, expf 5.60 vs 103.80 = 18.5x on Xeon w9-3495X, etc.), and the benchmark code is public (test/log_v.cpp, test/exp_v.cpp compare std::log / std::exp array loops). The readme does not say which compiler or flags produced the numbers, so it falls short of A.

corrections.caveats: GitHub's license detector reports no LICENSE file (license: null). BSD-3-Clause ('modified new BSD license') is stated in readme.md and in the include/fmath.h header comment, but there is no standalone LICENSE file. The benchmark tables give CPU model and OS but not the compiler or flags. The repo's build scripts use Makefile CFLAGS -O2 and, on Windows, mk.bat with MSVC cl /O2 /arch:AVX2, but the readme does not tie the numbers to them. The readme warns the functions are slow for n < 16.

notes: All six speedups match readme.md exactly. The Windows rows were probably built with MSVC (mk.bat uses cl.exe) and the Linux rows with default CC/CXX at -O2. The readme does not say this, so baseline_stdlib and compiler_and_flags are left unchanged.

tier_reason: The first-party dev.to post (Feb 2023) includes benchmark code inline and states MSVC 19.33 and a Ryzen 9 3950X. Flags are given only as 'Default settings', so build config and optimization level are unknown. That makes it C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page reports 'Speedup: 558.71%' for res = aa * bb - cc on 1000x1000 double arrays: STL (nested std::vector<std::vector<double>> loops) 1.589ms vs LibRapid Array 284.405us per iteration. The 558.71% figure is the time ratio, ~5.59x, not '558.71% faster' (derived from page data). The post's summary says 'a speedup of over 500%'.

notes: Numbers, compiler, CPU and OS all match the post. The only fix is the wording: 558.71% is the ratio (1.589ms / 284.405us = 5.587), not a percentage gain. Metadata checks out: MIT license, 179 stars, last commit 2025-08-21, so stale.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The project's refereed CHEP2013 paper (J. Phys.: Conf. Ser. 513 052027, open access) has Table 1 timing VDT against glibc 2.12 libm with GCC 4.8.1 on a Core i7-4770K. Benchmark code is public (progs/vdtPerfBenchmark.cpp), but optimization flags are not stated, so not A. The few >50x entries (vectorised Exp, Sinf/Cosf/Tanf) come from very slow glibc 2.12 timings the paper itself discusses; the headline scalar gains are 1.3-13x, so no cap was applied.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Table 1 (ns/call, glibc 2.12 libm vs VDT v0.3.6), scalar double: Exp 102.0 vs 8.00 (~12.8x), Log 32.28 vs 11.48 (~2.8x), Sin 77.77 vs 16.50 (~4.7x), Cos 77.60 vs 14.41 (~5.4x), Tan 89.69 vs 10.59 (~8.5x), Asin 21.25 vs 8.94 (~2.4x), Atan 15.56 vs 8.41 (~1.9x), Isqrt 5.66 vs 4.27 (~1.3x). Vectorised AVX2+fma, e.g. Log 1.47 ns (~22x). Scalar single-precision Expf, Logf and Isqrtf are slower than libm (8.01 vs 7.52, 11.93 vs 10.90, 1.87 vs 0.63). README table (i7-3930K): Exp 16.7 vs 6.1/3.8/2.9 (scalar/SSE/AVX, ~2.7x/4.4x/5.8x), Log 34.9 vs 12.5/5.7/4.2 (~2.8x/6.1x/8.3x), Tan 46.6 vs 12.5/6.3/5.6 (~3.7x/7.4x/8.3x). (derived from page data)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.8.1 (paper; optimization flags not stated). The README table states no compiler.
corrections.hardware: Paper: Intel Core i7-4770K @ 3.50GHz, Scientific Linux 6, glibc 2.12. README table: Intel Core i7-3930K @ 3.20GHz, Scientific Linux 6
corrections.workload: Paper: 5 million random inputs over each function's domain (at most [-5000,5000]), timings averaged over 250 repetitions, scalar and array signatures with SSE/AVX/AVX2/AVX2+FMA. README table: double-precision ns/call over [-5000,5000] ((0,5000] for isqrt, [-1,1] for asin/acos).
corrections.caveats: Baseline is an old glibc 2.12 libm; some libm timings (scalar exp 102 ns, sinf/cosf/tanf ~178 ns over [-5000,5000]) are pathological for that version and inflate a few ratios. Optimization flags are unstated in both paper and README. Scalar single-precision expf/logf/isqrtf are slower than libm. Functions are approximate (average ~0.1-0.5 LSB difference vs libm). Hardware is ~2012-2013.

notes: README numbers and the record's derived ratios are all correct. The tier moves to B because of the refereed CHEP2013 paper; the numbers now come from it. License confirmed as LGPL-3.0-or-later: Licence.txt says 'version 3 ... or (at your option) any later version', although GitHub reports NOASSERTION.

tier_reason: The blog post states g++ 4.9.3 with -O3 -std=c++14 on an Intel i7-4500U (Ubuntu 15.04) and graphs speed relative to std::priority_queue. The benchmark program is public in the repo (perf_benchmark.cpp, which includes <queue>), so this meets A.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-4500U, Ubuntu 15.04, 32KB L1d cache, 64-byte cache lines
corrections.caveats: Methodology (CPU, compiler, flags) is fully stated but dates from 2015 on old hardware. The post's text gives no numeric ratios, only relative graphs. The in-place std::pair<int, std::unique_ptr<msg>> layout gave mixed results, including 'examples of worse performance than std::priority_queue<>'; gains are consistent only for int payloads and the split priority/payload layouts. Mini-heap size 8 is consistently bad. The current perf_benchmark.cpp uses the tachymeter library and may differ from the 2015 version. The last commit (2025-09-18) is just over 12 months before this run.

notes: The qualitative quotes in claimed_speedup appear verbatim on the page. Metadata checks out: BSL-1.0, 111 stars, last commit 2025-09-18, so stale.

tier_reason: example/README.md states gcc 4.6.3 -O3 on an Intel Xeon E5-2690 and tables rheap vs std::priority_queue on DIMACS USA road graphs. The benchmark code is public (example/benchmark_dijkstra_main.cc: 100 random sources, averaged).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Pure priority-queue workload: 1.40-1.74x faster (e.g. USA-road-t.USA.gr: rheap 1.302186 vs stl 2.266316; USA-road-d.USA.gr: 1.222667 vs 2.119727). Overall Dijkstra time including edge traversal: ~1.12-1.29x faster (e.g. NY-d 0.024032 vs 0.027614, USA-t 3.817832 vs 4.934690). (derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: Benchmark dates from 2015 on hardware and a compiler of that era. There is no standalone LICENSE file, but the root README.md contains the full MIT License text ('Copyright (c) 2015 Takuya Akiba'). The root README's 'about 2X faster' is rounded up from the measured maximum of ~1.74x. Speedup grows with graph size (smallest on the 264K-vertex NY graph). No commits since 2015.

notes: The overall-time range was misstated: the smaller graphs show only ~1.12-1.15x, so the range is 1.12-1.29x, not 1.25-1.29x. The license is MIT (full text in README), so usability becomes copyable. All other metadata checks out: 67 stars, last commit 2015-05-16, abandoned.
